commitResults.messageTitle: Add assertions to check for important assumptions in the app
commitResults.messageBody:
- Parser The command matches the input prefix, ensuring the helper removes the correct prefix

- TaskList.add Successful additions stay within 100 tasks, confirming the capacity check worked

- TaskList.delete Deletion reduces the count by exactly one, preserving consistent task numbering

- MarkCommand The task becomes marked before saving or reporting success

- UnmarkCommand The task becomes unmarked before saving or reporting success

Parser.parseEvent combines marker checks, substring extraction, and
blank-value checks in compound conditions, then extracts the same date
fields again when constructing the event. Understanding the guards
requires tracing short-circuit evaluation and index arithmetic together.

This is a high-priority readability issue because these conditions
decide whether user input is safe to parse and which error is shown.
Future changes can accidentally alter validation order or access an
invalid substring range. The course's Avoid Complicated Expressions
guideline recommends separating such expressions into named steps.

Introduce named marker checks and extract each trimmed date field once.
Use an empty field when its markers are missing or reversed, then apply
the existing missing-date checks. This makes the safety conditions
explicit without adding new classes or a general parsing framework.

Preserve accepted inputs, error messages, validation order, and saved
task data. In particular, check for an end date before a start date,
and check the task name before converting either date.

Add regression tests for blank and adjacent markers, reversed markers,
error precedence, invalid calendar dates, whitespace, and recovery.
Extend the UI plan to verify that rejected events leave tasks unchanged.

Validation: Gradle check passes all 78 JUnit tests on Java 25. All 18
console UI cases pass with assertions enabled, and diff checks pass.

Storage.parseTask uses raw array positions and string literals to decode
each saved task. Values such as parts[3] and parts[4] reveal neither the
meaning of a field nor its place in the persistence format. A reader must
mentally reconstruct the schema before checking the parsing logic.

This makes storage maintenance risky because swapping two indices still
compiles and can assign the wrong date or name to a task. The course's
Avoid Magic Numbers and Avoid Magic Literals guidelines recommend giving
such domain values descriptive names.

Introduce constants for the field separator, marked status, task codes,
and field positions used by the saved-task schema. Use those constants in
parseTask so each access states which value it retrieves.

Keep the file format and parsing behavior unchanged. Strengthen the
storage test to verify that completion status, names, and every date field
are mapped to the expected task properties.

Validation: Gradle check passes all 78 JUnit tests on Java 25. All 18
console UI cases pass with assertions enabled, and diff checks pass.

TaskList retains the exact ArrayList supplied by its caller. Code outside
the class can therefore clear, reorder, or add tasks without using the
TaskList operations that enforce its rules. The constructor also requires
a concrete collection type even though it only needs List behavior.

This hidden sharing weakens encapsulation and makes changes difficult to
trace. A caller modifying its own list should not silently mutate an
already-created TaskList or bypass the task limit.

Accept the List interface and copy its contents into TaskList-owned
storage. Update Storage to return the same abstraction so both classes
describe the capability they require instead of a particular
implementation.

Add a regression test that mutates the source collection after
construction and verifies that the TaskList remains unchanged. Keep all
console behavior and the saved-data format unchanged.

Validation: Gradle check passes all 79 JUnit tests on Java 25. All 18
console UI cases pass with assertions enabled, and diff checks pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Move occurrence rules into task types
commitResults.messageBody:
TaskList determines whether a task occurs on a date by inspecting its
concrete type and reading subtype-specific fields. This gives the list
two responsibilities: managing tasks and knowing the date semantics of
every task subtype.

The type checks make the design harder to extend because every new dated
task requires another branch in TaskList. They also place deadline and
event rules away from the classes that own the relevant dates. This
mixes abstraction levels and makes the code's responsibilities less
obvious.

Define occursOn as part of Task behavior. Basic tasks return false,
deadlines compare their due date, and events apply their inclusive date
range. TaskList can then filter all tasks through one polymorphic call.

Add focused tests for undated tasks, deadline matches, event boundaries,
inside dates, and surrounding dates. Keep displayed output, filtering
results, and saved data unchanged.

Validation: Gradle check passes all 82 JUnit tests on Java 25. All 18
console UI cases pass with assertions enabled, and diff checks pass.

Parser helpers receive the full user input and each removes its command
word using a hard-coded length. This duplicates argument extraction and
couples every helper to the dispatcher's command spelling. A command
rename can therefore leave parsing code compiling but slicing input at
the wrong position.

The repeated low-level string manipulation also obscures the main story
in parse: identify a command, obtain its arguments, and build the matching
Command object. This conflicts with the Single Level of Abstraction
Principle and makes the parser harder to review safely.

Extract the argument text once beside the command word and pass it to the
specialized helpers. Name the date markers used inside deadline and event
arguments, while retaining the public parseShowDate entry point for
callers that parse a complete show command.

Keep command recognition, whitespace handling, validation order, error
messages, dates, and stored task names unchanged. Extend parser and
command tests to cover names containing command words and recovery after
invalid inputs.

Validation: Gradle check passes all 83 JUnit tests on Java 25. All 18
console UI cases pass with assertions enabled, and diff checks pass.

Storage.parseTask uses the switch default branch to create a todo. As a
result, every unknown task code is accepted as if it were the supported
todo code, silently changing the meaning of malformed or newer data.

There is no legitimate default task type in the save-file format. The
course's Use the Default Branch guideline says that a default branch
should detect an error when no default action exists. Explicit handling
also makes the complete set of supported task codes visible to readers.

Add an explicit todo case and make the default branch report an I/O
error. This reuses Fifi's existing startup fallback for unreadable data
and leaves the unsupported file untouched instead of rewriting it under
the wrong type.

Add unit coverage that alternates valid and unsupported data to verify
both rejection and recovery. Extend the UI plan to ensure the chatbot
still starts, does not display a fabricated todo, and preserves the
source file.

Validation: Gradle check passes all 84 JUnit tests on Java 25. All 19
console UI cases pass with assertions enabled, and diff checks pass.

Task is used as a common base for Todo, Deadline, and Event, but it can
also be instantiated directly and supplies the todo storage format. This
creates a misleading fourth task form and lets future subclasses inherit
the "T" type code without choosing a persistence representation.

The task fields are also protected even though subclasses use the public
and protected behavior provided by Task. This exposes mutable completion
state more widely than required and allows subclasses to bypass the
methods that manage it.

Make Task abstract and require concrete task types to implement their own
file representation. Move todo serialization into ToDo, where the "T"
format belongs, and restrict task and date fields to private scope. Mark
dates final because they do not change after construction.

Adapt the shared Task tests to use a minimal concrete test implementation.
Keep task marking, display output, saved data, and date behavior unchanged.

Validation: Gradle check passes all 84 JUnit tests on Java 25. All 19
console UI cases pass with assertions enabled, and diff checks pass.

Mark, unmark, and delete convert the user's one-based task number into a
zero-based list position. The converted value is still named taskNumber
throughout the parser, commands, and TaskList, even though those two
concepts differ by one.

This name is misleading at the exact boundary where off-by-one errors are
most likely. The course's Avoid Misleading Names guideline recommends
names that describe an entity accurately and distinguish related values
with different meanings.

Rename the converted value and related methods to taskIndex from the
point of conversion through list access. Update Javadocs to use the same
term so the code and its contract describe one consistent concept.

Strengthen command tests to verify that mark and unmark update only the
selected task. Keep user-facing numbering, command syntax, output, and
saved data unchanged.

Validation: Gradle check passes all 84 JUnit tests on Java 25. All 19
console UI cases pass with assertions enabled, and diff checks pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Track task creation and completion times
commitResults.messageBody:
Task statistics need a reliable way to identify when a task was created and when it was most recently completed. The previous save format only recorded the current completion state, so that information was lost between runs.

Let's record creation and last-completion timestamps for every task and persist them alongside the existing task fields.

Keep legacy data files readable by treating missing timestamps as unknown. Retain the last-completion time when a task is unmarked, and replace it when the task is marked again, so the stored history matches the latest completion action.

A raw completed-task count does not explain which work needs attention. Deadlines and events also need status rules that respect their dates while keeping every task in exactly one category.

Let's calculate totals, completion rate, todo completion, pending and overdue deadlines, and upcoming, ongoing, and past events as of a supplied time.

Support an inclusive creation-date filter for period statistics and report legacy tasks that are excluded because their creation time is unknown. Supplying the reference time also keeps boundary behavior deterministic in tests.

Users need to view the calculated status breakdown in the JavaFX chat interface and choose whether it covers the full list or tasks created during a specific period.

Let's add stats, stats all, and stats since yyyy-MM-dd commands that return one readable multiline response. Use Past for unfinished events whose end date has passed, and explain when legacy tasks cannot be included in a dated report.

Validate unsupported period syntax with actionable guidance and cover command parsing, GUI responses, category output, date filtering, and legacy-data behavior in automated and console UI tests.

The statistics branch passes its tests, but the CI check fails because several test method names and wrapped lambda expressions do not follow the configured Checkstyle rules.

Let's shorten the affected test names to the permitted structure and keep lambda parameter parentheses on the same line as their method call.

These changes preserve test behavior while allowing the full Gradle check to pass on every CI platform.

Users cannot assess task progress or schedule status from the task list
alone, and dated reports require creation and completion timestamps that
survive application restarts

Let's merge task timestamp persistence and task statistics into master

The feature keeps legacy data readable, groups todos, deadlines, and
events into mutually exclusive status categories, and supports both
all-time reports and reports for tasks created since a specified date
Statistics appear as a readable multiline response in the GUI

A statistics period that starts after today cannot contain historical task activity, but the command accepts it and displays an empty report. This makes an invalid request look like a valid result.

Let's reject future start dates for stats since reports and tell users to enter today or an earlier date.

Keep the validation in the statistics command so date parsing remains reusable for future deadlines, events, and schedule searches.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add response objects with per-command error status
commitResults.messageBody:
GUI responses contain only text, so the frontend cannot reliably
distinguish an error from a successful response.

Let's return immutable ChatResponse objects from getChatResponse while
retaining getResponse for callers that only need text. Capture failures
through a dedicated error method so message wording does not determine
whether the GUI treats a response as an error.

Handle out-of-range task numbers as recoverable errors. They otherwise
escape command handling and prevent the frontend from showing guidance.

Cover invalid/valid command sequences, saved-state preservation, empty
task lists, and save failures. Gradle check passes 112 JUnit tests and
Checkstyle on Java 25; all 26 console UI cases pass with assertions enabled.

commitResults.messageTitle: Highlight command errors in the GUI and console
commitResults.messageBody:
Errors use the same presentation as successful messages, making it easy
to overlook invalid input or a failed save.

Let's use the response error status to show a pale red message box with
a dark red border, readable text, and a bold Error heading. Keep styles
in a bundled stylesheet and preserve normal replies and user messages.
Add an [ERROR] heading to console failures for equivalent visibility.

Update the user guide and expected console transcripts. JavaFX tests
check error styling, multiline wrapping, and valid replies after errors.
Presentation tests skip Linux environments without a graphical display.

Validation on Java 25: all 116 JUnit tests, Checkstyle, and 26 console UI
cases pass. The bundled JAR passes a GUI smoke check of actual Main input
handling, stylesheet loading, error recovery, input clearing, and exit.

commitResults.messageTitle: Validate commands and recover from bad input
commitResults.messageBody:
Malformed parameters and ignored command arguments can produce confusing
errors or accidentally exit the application. Unsafe descriptions can also
break the saved task format.

Let's validate parameter boundaries, repeated parameters, positive task
numbers, supported calendar dates, event ordering, and description text.
Accept surrounding whitespace and tabs while preserving task descriptions.
Reject extra arguments to list and bye, and exit cleanly at console EOF.

Extend recovery tests and the console plan with incorrect commands followed
by valid commands. All 123 JUnit tests and 28 console cases pass on Java 25.

commitResults.messageTitle: Reject new tasks with duplicate details
commitResults.messageBody:
Repeated task entries make task numbers and completion statistics harder
to interpret. Completion status should not allow an identical task to be
added again.

Let's compare task type, trimmed case-sensitive description, and relevant
dates before adding a task. Ignore completion status and timestamps, allow
different dates or types, and preserve duplicates already saved by older
versions. Deleting a task allows the same details to be added again.

Cover rejection, state preservation, distinct tasks, and recovery in JUnit
and the console plan. All 126 JUnit tests and 29 console cases pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Protect saved tasks when loading fails
commitResults.messageBody:
Malformed saved records can crash startup, silently change task details,
or leave an empty list that later overwrites the unreadable file.

Let's validate legacy and timestamped record shapes, status values,
descriptions, dates, timestamp ordering, and the task limit. Ignore blank
lines and identify the line containing invalid data without modifying it.
Guard task constructors so invalid task details cannot enter the model.

Show loading failures as highlighted errors in both interfaces and block
all task changes until the file is corrected and Fifi restarts. Missing
files still support first use, and read-only commands remain available.

Extend corruption, recovery, boundary, and environment-failure tests.
All 133 JUnit tests and 31 console cases pass on Java 25.

commitResults.messageTitle: Preserve task state when saving fails
commitResults.messageBody:
Commands change live tasks before writing the save file, so a failed save
leaves unsaved additions, deletions, or completion timestamps in memory.
Writing directly to the save file also risks losing its previous contents.

Let's stage changes on independent task copies and commit the live list
and success response only after saving succeeds. Write a complete file in
the same directory and replace the save file atomically. Preserve the old
file if replacement fails or atomic moves are unsupported, and clean up
failed temporary saves without hiding the original failure.

Reject completion before a known creation time with clock-recovery advice,
and keep saved timestamp years within the supported range. Explain safe
retry and recovery in the user guide.

Test denied replacement, unsupported atomic moves, unchanged timestamps,
cleanup, successful retries, and GUI startup warnings. All 138 JUnit tests,
33 console cases, and Checkstyle checks pass on Java 25.
